earbuds.title: Market for wireless earbuds
earbuds.body: In the market for wireless earbuds, the inverse demand function is **P = 240 − 3Q** and the inverse supply function is **P = 40 + 2Q**, where P is price in dollars and Q is quantity in thousands of units per month.

questions.prompt: The Supply and Demand framework assumes perfect competition. According to the slides, which of the following is **NOT** one of the underlying assumptions?
options: Firms can enter or exit the market easily
Each agent is small compared to the overall market and cannot change the market price
A single large firm can set the market price to maximize its own profit
There are many buyers and many sellers
questions.explanation: Perfect competition assumes many buyers/sellers, price-taking agents, each "small" relative to the market, and free entry/exit. A firm large enough to **set** the market price on its own contradicts the "small compared to the overall market" assumption — that describes market power, not perfect competition.

questions.prompt: According to the Law of Demand, holding every other factor constant, what happens to quantity demanded when the price of a good falls?
options: Quantity demanded increases
Quantity demanded decreases
Demand increases — the whole curve shifts right
Demand decreases — the whole curve shifts left
questions.explanation: The Law of Demand states that, ceteris paribus, a **decrease** in price raises **quantity demanded**. Options c and d confuse this own-price effect with a shift in demand, which the slides reserve for changes in factors *other than* the good's own price.

questions.prompt: A good's price falls. Using the slides' framing of the two effects behind the Law of Demand, which statement correctly distinguishes the substitution effect from the income effect?
options: Substitution effect: the good is now relatively cheaper, so consumers switch to buying this good instead of others; Income effect: consumers can now afford to buy more than before with the same income
Substitution effect: consumers can now afford to buy more than before with the same income; Income effect: consumers switch to buying other goods instead
Both effects describe consumers switching to substitute goods when the price changes
Both effects describe a fixed income buying strictly less as the price falls
questions.explanation: Per the slides: the **substitution effect** is switching toward a good that is now relatively cheaper; the **income effect** is being able to afford more with the same fixed income. Option b swaps these two definitions, and c/d each collapse both effects into only one of them.

questions.prompt: The demand function is Q<sub>D</sub> = a − bP. When rewritten in inverse form P = c − dQ<sub>D</sub> for graphing, how are c and d related to a and b?
options: c = a/b and d = 1/b
c = b/a and d = b
c = a − b and d = a/b
c = ab and d = 1/a
questions.explanation: The slides define the inverse demand function as P = c − dQ<sub>D</sub>, where **c = a/b** (the vertical intercept) and **d = 1/b** (the slope). This is why price sits on the vertical axis of the demand curve even though it is the independent variable in Q<sub>D</sub> = a − bP.

questions.prompt: The price of a good rises while every other factor affecting demand stays the same. What does this cause, according to the slides?
options: A change in the quantity demanded — a movement along the existing demand curve
A change in demand — the demand curve shifts left
A change in demand — the demand curve shifts right
Both the demand curve and the supply curve shift
questions.explanation: The slides define a movement along the demand curve (a **change in quantity demanded**) as caused specifically by a change in the good's *own* price. A **shift** (change in demand) is instead caused by other factors like income or population — none of which changed here.

questions.prompt: According to the slides, which of the following would cause the demand curve for good X to shift outward (increase)?
options: A reduction in interest rates
An increase in interest rates
An increase in the price of a complementary good Z
A decrease in the price of a substitute good Y
questions.explanation: The slides list a **reduction in interest rates** as a factor that increases demand — cheaper borrowing supports more spending, so D shifts outward. A **rise** in interest rates, a pricier complement, or a cheaper substitute are each listed as demand **decreasers** instead.

questions.prompt: Why does the supply curve slope upward, according to the slides?
options: Because producers' costs rise as they produce more, so firms need higher prices to cover those costs
Because consumers are willing to pay more when a good is scarce
Because producers prefer to sell less at higher prices
Because the substitution effect makes producers switch to other goods
questions.explanation: The slides state the supply curve is a **direct representation of producers' costs**: costs rise as output rises, so firms must charge higher prices to cover them — this gives the Law of Supply its upward slope. Option b describes consumer willingness to pay, a demand-side idea, not the supply relationship.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would cause the supply curve for good X to shift inward (decrease), according to the slides?
options: Interest rates rise
Production technology improves
The number of firms increases
Cheaper alternative inputs become available
questions.explanation: Rising interest rates raise firms' borrowing costs and are listed as a supply **decreaser**, shifting S inward. Improved technology, more firms, and cheaper alternative inputs are all listed as supply **increasers** — the opposite effect on the curve.

questions.prompt: At a market price below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied — a shortage (excess demand). According to the slides, how will producers respond?
options: Raise prices and expand production until equilibrium is reached
Cut prices and cut production until equilibrium is reached
Keep prices unchanged since the market self-corrects without producer action
Reduce production now to build inventory for future demand
questions.explanation: The slides state that at a shortage, producers notice unserved customers and respond by **raising prices and expanding production** until reaching equilibrium. Option b describes the correct response to a **surplus** (excess supply) at a price *above* equilibrium instead.

questions.topic: Demand vs supply shifts on P and Q
questions.prompt: According to the slides, which statement correctly describes how equilibrium price and quantity respond to shifts in demand versus shifts in supply?
options: A demand shift moves price and quantity in the same direction; a supply shift moves them in opposite directions
A demand shift moves price and quantity in opposite directions; a supply shift moves them in the same direction
Both demand and supply shifts always move price and quantity in the same direction
Both demand and supply shifts always move price and quantity in opposite directions
questions.explanation: The slides state that when **demand** shifts, price and quantity always move **together** (both rise or both fall); when **supply** shifts, they move in **opposite** directions. Options c and d each erase this distinction, and b reverses it entirely.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. What is the equilibrium quantity Q*, in thousands of units?

answer.hint: Set the two prices equal and solve for Q.

questions.explanation: Set the two curves equal: 240 − 3Q = 40 + 2Q → 200 = 5Q → **Q\* = 40** (thousand units). Checking either curve at Q = 40 gives the same price, confirming equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. What is the equilibrium price P*, in dollars?
questions.explanation: Substitute Q\* = 40 into either curve: P = 240 − 3(40) = **$120**, or P = 40 + 2(40) = $120. Both curves agree, confirming the equilibrium price.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. If the market price were $90 instead of the equilibrium price, what would be the size of the shortage, in thousands of units?

answer.hint: Compare Q<sub>D</sub> and Q<sub>S</sub> at P = 90.

questions.explanation: At P = 90: Q<sub>D</sub> = (240 − 90)/3 = **50**; Q<sub>S</sub> = (90 − 40)/2 = **25**. Since Q<sub>D</sub> > Q<sub>S</sub>, there is a shortage of 50 − 25 = **25** (thousand units) — producers will raise price and expand output toward equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. The demand function can also be written as Q<sub>D</sub> = 80 − (1/3)P. In the inverse form P = c − dQ<sub>D</sub>, what is the value of d?

answer.hint: d = 1/b, where b is the coefficient on P.

questions.explanation: With Q<sub>D</sub> = a − bP, here a = 80 and b = 1/3. The slides give **d = 1/b** = 1/(1/3) = **3**, which matches the −3Q term already used in P = 240 − 3Q for this scenario.

questions.prompt: The population of consumers for good X grows. Draw the new demand curve D₂ and mark the new equilibrium E₂.

tasks.label: D₂
tasks.prompt: Draw the new demand curve D₂

questions.explanation: Population growth raises the number of buyers, increasing demand for X at **every** price — the whole curve shifts right to D₂. Supply is unchanged, so the market slides up along S₁: equilibrium **price rises** (P₂ > P₁) and equilibrium **quantity rises** (Q₂ > Q₁).

questions.prompt: Interest rates rise, making it more expensive for consumers to finance purchases of good X on credit. Draw the new demand curve D₂ and mark the new equilibrium E₂.

tasks.label: D₂
tasks.prompt: Draw the new demand curve D₂

questions.explanation: Higher interest rates raise the cost of financing purchases, decreasing demand for X at **every** price — the whole curve shifts left to D₂. Supply is unchanged, so the market slides down along S₁: equilibrium **price falls** (P₂ < P₁) and equilibrium **quantity falls** (Q₂ < Q₁).

questions.prompt: Several firms exit the industry, reducing the number of firms producing good X. Draw the new supply curve S₂ and mark the new equilibrium E₂.

tasks.label: S₂
tasks.prompt: Draw the new supply curve S₂

questions.explanation: Fewer firms in the industry means less is supplied at **every** price — the whole curve shifts left to S₂. Demand is unchanged, so along D₁ the new equilibrium has a **higher price** (P₂ > P₁) and a **lower quantity** (Q₂ < Q₁) — price and quantity move in **opposite** directions, as supply shifts always do.

questions.prompt: The demand curve is P = 200 − 4Q. Mark the point on the demand curve showing the quantity demanded when the price is $120.

tasks.label: Q at $120
tasks.prompt: Place the point on D where P = $120

questions.explanation: Solve 120 = 200 − 4Q → 4Q = 80 → **Q = 20**. This is a movement *along* the existing demand curve, caused by a change in the good's own price — the curve itself does not shift.
